planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light shade; Gentle Shepherd is a classic near-white daylily prized for its clear, pale color and ruffled form.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light shade. Gentle Shepherd bears large, ruffled, near-white blooms with a soft chartreuse-green throat, one of the palest and most consistently near-white daylilies available, opening on sturdy scapes above a full clump of arching foliage. Its light color makes it a favorite for moon gardens and evening viewing, where it glows in low light. Deadhead spent blooms daily for a tidy appearance, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to maintain vigorous bloom.

common_name: Snow Hill Salvia (White-Flowered Compact Meadow Sage)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Snow Hill is a compact white-flowered meadow sage, an uncommon color among Salvia nemorosa cultivars.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun. Snow Hill bears dense spikes of clean white flowers on a compact, tidy plant, a rare white-flowered selection among the typically blue and violet Salvia nemorosa cultivars, useful for cooling down a hot-colored border or pairing crisply with silver foliage. Shear spent flower spikes back by half after the first flush to encourage a strong rebloom later in the season. It is drought-tolerant once established and needs little care beyond occasional deadheading and dividing congested clumps every few years.

common_name: Marcus Salvia (Dwarf Violet-Blue Compact Meadow Sage)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Marcus is one of the most compact Salvia nemorosa cultivars available, useful for small borders and edging.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun. Marcus forms a very compact, dense mound topped with abundant violet-blue flower spikes, notably smaller and tidier than most meadow sage cultivars, making it a good choice for edging, rock gardens, or the front of a border where taller salvias would flop or crowd neighbors. Shear spent flower spikes back by half after the first flush to encourage a strong rebloom later in the season. It is drought-tolerant once established and needs little care beyond occasional deadheading.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Rose Queen is a classic older cultivar bearing rose-pink flower spikes, an unusual color among meadow sage cultivars.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun. Rose Queen bears dense spikes of rose-pink flowers on a sturdy, upright plant, a warmer, softer color than the blue and violet tones that dominate most Salvia nemorosa cultivars, pairing well with silver foliage and other pastel perennials. Shear spent flower spikes back by half after the first flush to encourage a strong rebloom later in the season. It is drought-tolerant once established and needs little care beyond occasional deadheading and dividing congested clumps every few years.

common_name: Wesuwe Salvia (Early Long-Blooming Deep Violet-Blue Meadow Sage)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Wesuwe is an early-blooming, long-flowering Salvia nemorosa cultivar with deep violet-blue spikes.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun. Wesuwe bears dense spikes of deep violet-blue flowers, opening earlier in spring than many meadow sage cultivars and continuing over an unusually long season, especially with prompt deadheading. Its sturdy, upright habit and rich color make it a reliable anchor for the front or middle of a sunny border. Shear spent flower spikes back by half after the first flush to encourage a strong rebloom, and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Argentine Skies Salvia (Pale Sky-Blue Anise Sage)

planting.note: Plant container plants after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Argentine Skies is a pale-flowered form of anise sage, cooler in tone than the popular Black and Blue cultivar.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Argentine Skies bears pale, powdery sky-blue flowers with pale green calyces, a much softer, cooler-toned selection of anise sage than the deep cobalt-and-black-calyx Black and Blue cultivar, useful for pastel garden schemes or as a gentler backdrop for bolder companions. Like other anise sage it grows from tuberous roots, dying back after frost and resprouting in spring, and spreads by underground stolons into a substantial colony over time. Cut plants to the ground in late winter and it will resprout vigorously, drawing hummingbirds from summer through frost.
